title: BGP Extended Communities Attribute
summary: Defines the extended community attribute for BGP-4, a mechanism for labeling information carried in BGP. The labels can control how routing information is distributed or serve other applications. It is standards-track and was later updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606.

plainLanguage.summary: Sticky notes attached to route announcements, telling routers how to treat them. These notes have room for more kinds of instructions.

questions: what is a route target in bgp
what is the bgp extended communities attribute type code
how big is a bgp extended community
subtitle: A structured, 8-octet label that BGP routes can carry, so operators can filter and steer routes by type.

tldr.problem: The existing BGP Community attribute has a limited value range and no structure, so communities can overlap and policy has to list every value explicitly.
tldr.mechanism: The Extended Communities attribute (Type Code 16) carries a set of 8-octet values. Each has a Type field that says how the value is laid out and whether it is transitive across AS boundaries.
tldr.outcome: Operators can filter or accept routes by community type and carry Route Target and Route Origin labels. The RFC was later updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606.

today: RFC 4360 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606, so read it together with those documents. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Extend BGP Communities
sections.content:
The Extended Community Attribute is a way to label information carried in BGP-4. Those labels can control how the information is distributed, or serve other applications. It improves on the older BGP Community Attribute (RFC 1997) in two ways.

First, it has an extended range, so communities can be assigned for many uses without fear of overlap. Second, it adds a Type field that gives the community space some structure.

Structure matters for policy. With it, a router can filter out all communities of one type, or allow only certain values for one type. It can also say whether a community is transitive or non-transitive across an Autonomous System (AS) boundary. Without structure, the only option is to list every allowed or denied value by hand.
sections.plainLanguage: The old labels were like numbered stickers with no categories. The new labels have a category on them, so a router can say 'ignore every sticker of this kind' in one rule.

sections.title: The Attribute and Its Type Field
sections.content:
The Extended Communities Attribute is a transitive optional BGP attribute with Type Code 16. It holds a set of extended communities, and every route carrying it belongs to all the communities listed.

Each extended community is an 8-octet quantity: a Type field of 1 or 2 octets, then a Value field with the remaining octets. There are two classes of type. A Regular type has a 1-octet Type field. An Extended type has a 2-octet Type field. The class is not encoded in the type itself. It is set by the document that defines the type and by the IANA registry.

The high-order octet of the Type field has two flag bits. The I bit is the IANA authority bit. Value 0 means the type is assignable by IANA under the First Come First Served policy. Value 1 means part of that space is assignable under Standards Action or Early IANA Allocation, and the rest is for Experimental use. The T bit is the transitive bit. Value 0 means the community is transitive across ASes, and value 1 means it is non-transitive. The other 6 bits indicate the structure of the community.

Two extended communities are equal only when all 8 octets are equal.
sections.plainLanguage: Every label is exactly 8 bytes long. The first byte or two say what kind of label it is and whether it may travel past your network's border. The rest holds the actual message.

sections.title: Three Defined Value Layouts
sections.content:
The RFC defines three extended types as templates. The high-order octet of the Type field picks the template, and the low-order octet is a sub-type that says which particular kind of community it is. Each has a 2-octet Type field and a 6-octet Value field.

  • Two-Octet AS Specific (high octet 0x00 or 0x40): a 2-octet Global Administrator holding an AS number assigned by IANA, and a 4-octet Local Administrator that the organization owning that AS can use for any information.
  • IPv4 Address Specific (high octet 0x01 or 0x41): a 4-octet Global Administrator holding an IPv4 unicast address assigned by one of the Internet registries, and a 2-octet Local Administrator that the address holder can use as it likes.
  • Opaque (high octet 0x03 or 0x43): a generic type whose 6-octet Value field is defined by a sub-type to be assigned by IANA.

In the first two layouts, the format and meaning of the Local Administrator value should be defined by the sub-type of the community.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three label templates. One has your network's number and a note you write yourself. One has your network's address and a shorter note. The third is a blank template for other uses.

sections.title: Route Target and Route Origin
sections.content:
Two communities are defined using these templates. Both are of an extended type and both are transitive across the AS boundary.

The Route Target community identifies one or more routers that may receive a set of routes carrying it. Its low-order Type octet is 0x02. The Route Origin community identifies one or more routers that inject a set of routes into BGP. Its low-order Type octet is 0x03.

For both, the high-order octet can be 0x00, 0x01 or 0x02. With 0x00 or 0x02, the Local Administrator holds a number from a numbering space run by the organization that was assigned the AS number in the Global Administrator sub-field. With 0x01, it is a number from a space run by the organization that was assigned the IP address in the Global Administrator sub-field.

The RFC points to RFC 4364 as one possible use of both communities.
sections.plainLanguage: One label says 'these routes may be delivered to these routers'. The other says 'these routes started at these routers'. Both are allowed to cross the border between networks.

sections.title: How Routers Handle the Attribute
sections.content:
A BGP speaker may use the attribute to control which routing information it accepts or distributes to its peers. It MUST NOT use it to change best path selection in a way that leads to forwarding loops.

A speaker that receives a route without the attribute MAY add it when passing the route on. A speaker that receives a route with it MAY modify it according to local policy.

For aggregation, by default, when routes are aggregated and the aggregate does not carry the ATOMIC_AGGREGATE attribute, the aggregate should carry the set union of all the extended communities of the aggregated routes. Local configuration can override this.

A non-transitive community SHOULD be removed before a route is advertised across an AS boundary, but SHOULD NOT be removed when crossing a BGP Confederation boundary. A route can carry both the old Communities attribute and the Extended Communities attribute. Each is handled by its own specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can add, change or read these labels when they pass routes along. Labels marked 'stay home' get peeled off at the border, and when several routes are merged into one, the merged route keeps all their labels.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Type Ranges
sections.content:
IANA created a registry called "BGP Extended Communities Type". A regular type gets an 8-bit value and an extended type gets a 16-bit value. A value allocated for a regular type MUST NOT be reused as the high-order octet of an extended type, and the reverse also holds. Each request must say whether the type is transitive or non-transitive.

Future assignments use Standards Action, Early IANA Allocation, or First Come First Served. The ranges are split by class and transitivity. For example, regular transitive types use 0x90-0xbf for Standards Action or Early Allocation and 0x00-x3f for First Come First Served. Values 0x80-0x8f and 0xc0-0xcf (regular), and 0x8000-0x8fff and 0xc000-0xcfff (extended), are for Experimental use.

The RFC also creates registries for the three classes: Two-octet AS Specific, IPv4 Address Specific and Opaque, all assigned First Come First Served. It makes four initial assignments, listed below.
sections.plainLanguage: A central office keeps the official list of label kinds so nobody reuses the same code for two things. Some codes are reserved for experiments.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says this extension has security implications similar to BGP Communities (RFC 1997) and does not change the underlying security issues.

An operator who relies on information carried in BGP must have a transitive trust relationship back to the source of that information. The RFC leaves the mechanisms that would provide such a relationship out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If you trust a label, you are trusting everyone who handled the letter before you. This memo does not fix that, it only says so.

fields.name: Sub-Type
fields.desc: Low-order octet of the type; indicates the sub-type.

fields.name: Global Administrator
fields.desc: An Autonomous System number assigned by IANA.

fields.name: Local Administrator
fields.desc: Any information chosen by the organization that owns the AS number.

fields.name: Sub-Type
fields.desc: Low-order octet of the type; indicates the sub-type.

fields.name: Global Administrator
fields.desc: An IPv4 unicast address assigned by one of the Internet registries.

fields.name: Local Administrator
fields.desc: Any information chosen by the organization that holds the address.

items.label: Two-octet AS specific Route Target
items.desc: Routers that may receive the routes.

items.label: Two-octet AS specific Route Origin
items.desc: Routers that inject the routes into BGP.

items.label: IPv4 address specific Route Target
items.desc: Same meaning, with an IPv4 address as the Global Administrator.

items.label: IPv4 address specific Route Origin
items.desc: Same meaning, with an IPv4 address as the Global Administrator.
